units.translation: 8 καὶ τὸ μὲν — κόλπον as above in L, where Jacoby deleted the last words : καὶ τὸ μὲν τῶν ῥείθρων εἰς τὸν Ἀδριατικὸν ἐκβάλλειν κόλπον, τὸ δὲ εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον πόντον in P
10 οὕτω — τοῦτο are read after ὀρῶν in line 7, whence W and Wil. transposed to this line
12 ἀνατολαῖς, namely of the Ister (Schneider)
13 πέμπουσιν in L : omitted in P; ἦχι in L : ἦχον in P
15 Σκύμνος — Ἴστρον are read before Ῥίπαια in line 11, transposed by W, deleted by Meineke
16 αὐτό Schwartz : -όν in L : omitted in P
17 τούτου in HF : -ων in L : τοῦ Ἴστρου in P
18 τὴν ἡμ. θάλ. in L : τὸν Ἀδριατικὸν κόλπον in P
22 στρωτ in L : σαυροτ- in P

They arrived. Hesiod (fr. 65 Rz.?) says that they sailed in through the Phasis. Hecataeus (1 fr. 18b J.) 〈... Artemidorus (see schol. 257/62b)〉 refuting him records that the Phasis does not flow out into the sea. Nor did they sail through the Tanais, but by the same route as before, as Sophocles in the Scythians (fr. 547 Pearson) records and Callimachus (fr. 377 Schn.). 〈...〉 of them, those who had sailed into the Adriatic did not find the Argonauts, but those who went through the Cyanean rocks to Corcyra, where they then were.

The Ister, flowing down from the Hyperboreans, when it reaches the region between Scythia and Thrace, splits into two, and one part of it empties into the Euxine Sea, the other into the Trinacrian sea.
c. μορμύρουσιν: they roar. Lᶢ P
d. The Trinacrian sea lies adjacent to Sicily; for it was formerly called Trinacria because it has three headlands, Pachynus, Lilybaeum, Pelorus. Lᵐ P

292-93a. γαίῃ ὅς ὑμετέρῃ: if it is written thus, γαίῃ ὅς ὑμετέρῃ, it will mean Hellas; for the Trinacrian sea lies adjacent to the land of the Greeks. But if it is ἡμετέρῃ, it will be the Ister; for this lies adjacent to the Colchians.
b. ὑμετέρης γαίης: the Achelous is the most distinguished of the other rivers of Hellas.
If then the Achelous is among you; for we hear the name. For Argus does not know that it is in their country.
He says, then, that the Ister rises again into the Achelous because it supplies its sources. L
295. αἴσιον: fitting. Lᶢ P
296. ὁλκός: the course of the star. Lᶢ (P)
301-02. ἐπεὶ πνοιαί τε: for the same gusts of winds remained and the heavenly brightness that appeared to them, signifying the voyage through the Ister.
Those who have written about the voyage of the Argonauts from Colchis disagree. 〈...〉 as also Callimachus (fr. 563 Schn.); but Apollonius says that they returned contrary to Callimachus.
303-06a. Κόλχοι δ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλοι: of the Colchians, some sailed through the Cyanean rocks, others with Apsyrtus made for the Ister. L
